Some research suggests that parental conflict — not divorce itself — is the key factor in children’s outcomes, meaning that divorce may in some cases be better for children than continuing an acrimonious marriage. Other research highlights the economic and social disadvantages associated with growing up in a lone parent household, including lower educational achievement and poorer health outcomes. Sociologists caution against treating all divorces as equally harmful, since outcomes vary significantly with income, quality of post-divorce parenting arrangements and the degree of continued conflict between former partners.

For the extended family, divorce disrupts grandparent–grandchild relationships and wider kinship networks. Grandparents on the non-resident parent’s side may lose contact with grandchildren. The rise of divorce has also contributed significantly to the growth of lone parent families in the UK, since many divorces involve children.

Serial monogamy describes the practice of having a succession of monogamous relationships or marriages — one at a time rather than simultaneously. As divorce has become more socially acceptable, more people go on to form new partnerships and remarry after divorce. Sociologists argue this reflects not a rejection of marriage as an institution but an individualisation of relationship choice. Some functionalists see serial monogamy as evidence that marriage remains highly valued — people seek it again after it breaks down rather than abandoning the institution.

An empty shell marriage, by contrast, is a marriage that persists legally but in which the couple have effectively separated emotionally, though they remain formally married. Empty shell marriages may persist for financial reasons (e.g. maintaining a joint mortgage), social reasons (e.g. religious objection to divorce) or for the perceived benefit of children. The concept is important because it shows that official divorce statistics undercount the number of relationships that have actually broken down.

Functionalist view: Parsons argued that the family adapts to meet social needs. From this perspective, rising divorce rates do not necessarily signal a “crisis” of the family but may reflect rising expectations of what marriage should provide. High remarriage rates suggest that marriage as an institution remains valued, even if individual marriages fail.

Feminist view: Most divorce petitions are filed by women, supporting the feminist argument that marriage has historically placed greater burdens on women. Rising divorce rates may reflect women’s growing economic independence and their capacity to leave unsatisfactory relationships. From this perspective, divorce is not a symptom of social breakdown but of women’s liberation from patriarchal constraints.

Marxist view: Marxists argue that the causes of marital breakdown are often rooted in the economic conditions of capitalism — poverty, financial stress and the alienation of work all increase pressure on family relationships. The increasing commodification of family life (consumer debt, housing insecurity) generates tensions that contribute to marital breakdown.

New Right view: Murray’s New Right perspective is critical of rising divorce rates, arguing that the growth of lone parent families resulting from divorce contributes to a dependency culture and the development of an underclass. The New Right argues that children raised without two parents are disadvantaged educationally and socially. This view has been challenged by feminist sociologists, who argue it pathologises lone parent families while ignoring the structural causes of their difficulties.

Key Fact

The main consequences of divorce include: financial hardship (particularly for women); social isolation (particularly for men); impacts on children’s educational and health outcomes; disruption of extended family relationships; and a significant increase in the number of lone parent families in the UK.

Why Is Researching Families Challenging?

Families are one of the most private social institutions. Unlike schools, workplaces or public spaces, families are largely closed to outside observation. This creates significant practical issues for sociologists who wish to study family life: gaining access, maintaining trust and capturing honest behaviour. At the same time, families involve deeply personal relationships — raising sensitive ethical issues around consent, confidentiality and the potential for harm. AQA requires students to evaluate research methods applied specifically to families, not just in the abstract.

Surveys and Questionnaires: Studying the Domestic Division of Labour

Surveys using questionnaires have been widely used to study the domestic division of labour and conjugal roles. Willmott and Young’s research for The Symmetrical Family (1973) used large-scale surveys to gather data from hundreds of households about how domestic tasks were divided. This quantitative approach allowed them to identify broad patterns and trends across social classes.

However, surveys have important limitations when used to study family life. Questionnaires produce data that is easily comparable and statistically analysable but may lack depth. Respondents may give socially desirable answers — describing a more equal division of tasks than actually exists — rather than recording their genuine behaviour. Ann Oakley criticised this limitation directly in her critique of Willmott and Young: their survey data on male domestic participation was based on a low threshold, and respondents may have overstated male involvement. Qualitative methods may better capture the complexity of domestic life than tick-box questionnaires.

Interviews: Gaining Depth on Family Experience

Oakley’s own research on housework used in-depth interviews with women about their experience of domestic labour. She used unstructured interviews, which allowed participants to speak freely in their own words about their experiences and feelings. This generated rich qualitative data about women’s attitudes to housework, their sense of identity and the emotional demands of domestic labour — data that a survey could not have captured.

Interviews have significant advantages for researching sensitive aspects of family life, such as experiences of domestic violence, parenting practices or the experience of divorce. They allow the researcher to probe for detail, follow up unexpected responses and build rapport with participants. However, they are also time-consuming and expensive, produce data that is difficult to generalise from a small sample, and rely on participants reporting their experiences honestly — which may be particularly problematic for sensitive topics within families.

Key Fact

Willmott and Young used large-scale surveys (quantitative) to study the domestic division of labour — allowing broad patterns to be identified but risking socially desirable responses. Oakley used in-depth unstructured interviews (qualitative) with women about housework — generating rich, detailed data but with a smaller, less generalisable sample.

Observation of Family Life

Observation of family life raises acute practical and ethical challenges. Observing family behaviour in its natural setting — the home — could provide highly valid data about how families actually behave (rather than what they say they do). However, gaining access to private family homes for observation is extremely difficult. Even when access is granted, families are likely to change their behaviour when they know they are being observed, creating a Hawthorne effect.

Participant observation — where the researcher lives with or becomes part of the family for a period — could generate highly naturalistic data, but raises serious ethical issues about intrusion into private life, the boundaries of the researcher’s role, and the potential for family members to feel pressured to participate. The Rapoports’ research on family diversity involved extensive contact with families over time, using a mixed methods approach combining interviews with observational elements.

Official Statistics on Families

Official statistics are a major source of data for studying family patterns. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes annual data on marriage rates, divorce rates, cohabitation, household composition, lone parent families and birth rates. The census collects detailed data on household composition every ten years.

Official statistics on divorce, marriage and family forms are quantitative, nationally representative and freely available, making them highly convenient for sociologists. However, they have significant limitations. Official statistics on families count legal arrangements (married couples, registered civil partnerships, legal divorces) but miss cohabiting couples who separate without legal proceedings and families that do not conform to standard administrative categories. Marriage and divorce statistics also change with legal reform (as the dramatic effect of the Divorce Reform Act 1969 demonstrates) — meaning trends in statistics may partly reflect changes in law rather than changes in family behaviour.

Practical issues include: access — families are private institutions and researchers cannot simply enter without invitation. Recruiting family research participants often requires working through schools, community centres, online networks or snowball sampling. Time and cost — longitudinal studies of families (tracking the same households over years or decades) are expensive and resource-intensive, though they yield valuable data on how families change. Representativeness — families that agree to participate in research may not be typical of all families (those experiencing serious domestic problems, for example, are less likely to volunteer for a study of “family life”). Changing composition — families change over time through births, deaths, divorce, remarriage and children leaving home, making longitudinal family research methodologically complex.

Key Fact

The AQA specification requires students to know three ethical issues in research: consent, confidentiality and harm. In family research, these apply with particular force: family members must all give informed consent; data about family relationships must be kept confidential; and researchers must consider the potential for their presence or questions to cause distress, particularly when studying sensitive topics such as domestic abuse, divorce or child neglect.

Informed consent is particularly complex when researching families with children. Children below the age of consent cannot legally give consent themselves, so parents or guardians must consent on their behalf. However, sociologists debate whether parental consent alone is sufficient — should children also give their assent? Children may feel unable to refuse to participate if their parents have agreed. Confidentiality is also challenging: if a researcher discovers evidence of child abuse or neglect during family research, they face a conflict between their duty of confidentiality to participants and their legal and moral obligation to protect the child from harm. AQA requires students to think about how ethical issues “can be addressed” — not just identified. Possible approaches include: briefing participants clearly about the limits of confidentiality before the study begins; using independent child welfare advisers; ensuring children can speak to researchers separately from parents.

What Is Education For?

Sociologists study education not just as a place where skills are taught, but as a social institution that shapes values, reproduces inequality and connects individuals to the wider society. Competing perspectives give very different answers to the question of what education is for — and whose interests it serves.

Key Fact

Functionalists argue that education performs three key functions for society: serving the needs of the economy, facilitating social mobility, and fostering social cohesion.

Durkheim: Transmission of Norms and Values

Functionalism begins from the assumption that social institutions exist because they serve a purpose. The French sociologist Émile Durkheim argued that education is the primary institution through which society transmits its values and norms to the next generation. Without this transmission, social solidarity — the glue that holds society together — would break down.

Durkheim identified two main functions of education. First, education creates social solidarity: by teaching a shared history, language and culture, schools turn individual children into citizens who feel they belong to the same community. Second, education teaches specialist skills that the economy needs — mathematics, literacy, technical knowledge — so that individuals can contribute to the division of labour in an industrialised society.

Parsons: Meritocracy and Achieved Status

American sociologist Talcott Parsons extended Durkheim’s analysis. Parsons argued that schools act as a “bridge” between the family and the wider society. In the family, a child is judged on particularistic standards — rules that apply only to that specific child, based on who they are. In wider society, however, people are judged on universalistic standards: the same rules apply to everyone, regardless of family background.

Parsons argued that schools prepare children for this shift by operating on meritocratic principles. In a meritocracy, exam results reflect genuine ability and effort. Students who work hard earn high grades and go on to high-status, well-paid jobs; those who do not earn lower grades and take less rewarding positions. The result is achieved status: people’s place in society reflects their own efforts, not their family background.

Students sometimes assume that a meritocracy means everyone ends up equal. It does not. Meritocracy means that unequal outcomes are fair because they reflect differences in effort and talent rather than background. Parsons’s point is that the inequality that results from a meritocracy is legitimate — it is earned. Critics from other perspectives challenge whether schools actually operate on meritocratic principles in practice.

The Marxist Critique: Education Serves Capitalism

Marxist sociologists challenge the functionalist view. From a Marxist perspective, education does not serve society as a whole but primarily serves the ruling class — the bourgeoisie. Rather than fostering genuine social cohesion, education reproduces the existing class hierarchy by disguising inequality as the result of individual merit.

Marxists argue that the “social solidarity” Durkheim describes is better understood as ideological control: schools teach working-class children to accept their subordinate position as natural and deserved. The hidden curriculum — the unwritten lessons about conformity, obedience and hierarchy — prepares working-class pupils for lives of routine employment. The claim that education facilitates social mobility is, for Marxists, largely a myth.

The Feminist Critique: A Gendered Institution

Feminist sociologists argue that the functionalist account ignores patriarchy. Historically, education was designed by and for men, preparing boys for paid work and public life while preparing girls for domestic roles. Even after formal barriers to entry were removed, feminists argue that schools continue to reproduce gender inequality through a gendered curriculum, teacher expectations and informal socialisation.

Functionalist: Education transmits shared values, creates social solidarity, teaches specialist skills and allocates roles meritocratically. Named theorists: Durkheim (social cohesion and specialist skills), Parsons (meritocracy and achieved status).

Marxist: Education reproduces class inequality, socialises workers into accepting exploitation, and presents ruling-class ideology as neutral common sense. The appearance of meritocracy legitimises an unequal system.

Feminist: Education reproduces gender inequality by channelling girls and boys into different subjects and career paths, reflecting and reinforcing a patriarchal society.

Interactionist: Rather than focusing on macro-level functions, interactionists examine how teacher expectations, labelling and pupil interactions shape individual outcomes within schools — a small-scale focus that functionalists and Marxists tend to overlook.

Key Fact

Parsons argued that schools bridge family and society by shifting children from particularistic standards (rules specific to the family) to universalistic standards (the same rules applied to everyone). This shift teaches children to compete on equal terms — the basis of a meritocracy.

lesson_title: Types of School and Alternative Provision
content_html:
Why Does School Type Matter?

The UK has a diverse education system. Different types of school reflect different political priorities — about selection, competition, the role of the market, and who education is for. Sociologists from different perspectives disagree about whether this diversity is a strength or a source of inequality.

Key Fact

The main types of school in the UK are: state-maintained primary and secondary schools, comprehensive schools, grammar schools, academies, free schools and private (independent) schools.

Primary and Secondary Schools

State education in England is divided into primary schools (ages 5–11) and secondary schools (ages 11–16 or 18). The vast majority of children attend state schools funded by central government and managed by local authorities or academy trusts. Compulsory state education was introduced in the nineteenth century and gradually extended; today all children in England must be in some form of education or training until the age of 18.

Comprehensive, Grammar and Selective Schools

Following the Education Act 1944, England adopted the tripartite system of grammar, technical and secondary modern schools, with pupils allocated by the eleven-plus examination. From the 1960s onwards, most local authorities replaced this with comprehensive schools, which accept pupils of all abilities. Comprehensive education was associated with the Labour Party and the principle that selection by ability at age eleven was unfair because it disadvantaged working-class children.

Grammar schools survive in some parts of England (notably Kent, Lincolnshire and parts of the West Midlands). Supporters argue that grammar schools provide high-achieving pupils from all backgrounds with access to a rigorous academic education. Critics — including many sociologists — argue that grammar schools entrench class inequality because middle-class families can afford private tuition to prepare their children for the eleven-plus, while working-class families typically cannot.

Academies and Free Schools

Academies were introduced under the Labour government in 2000 and significantly expanded by the Coalition government’s Academies Act 2010. Academies are state-funded but operate outside local authority control, with more freedom over curriculum, pay and admissions. Free schools were introduced in 2010 as a related policy: they can be set up by any group — parents, teachers, charities or faith organisations — and must be non-selective and non-fee-paying.

The expansion of academies and free schools is linked to the marketisation of education. The market logic assumes that competition between schools for pupils will drive up standards. Sociologist Stephen Ball has argued that marketisation benefits middle-class families who have the cultural capital and social networks to navigate school choice, while working-class families are disadvantaged.

Private Schools

Private schools — also called fee-paying, independent or public schools — are funded by fees paid by parents and private endowments rather than the state. Approximately 7% of pupils in England attend private schools. Sociologists note that this small minority produces a disproportionate share of senior politicians, judges, top civil servants and university entrants to highly selective institutions — raising questions about whether private schooling reinforces class inequality and limits social mobility.

Functionalist: A diverse range of school types allows the education system to match individuals to the roles that best suit their abilities, performing the meritocratic function of role allocation. Grammar schools and academies are seen as providing pathways for talented pupils.

Marxist: The existence of fee-paying private schools alongside state schools reflects and reinforces class inequality. The bourgeoisie purchase educational advantage for their children, ensuring that privileged positions in society are passed on across generations rather than earned on merit.

Feminist: Historically, many elite schools were single-sex institutions designed for boys. Feminists have highlighted how the expansion of co-educational comprehensive schooling improved girls’ access to the full curriculum, but argue that gender inequalities persist even within mixed schools through subject choices and teacher expectations.

New Right: Supporters of marketisation argue that parental choice and school competition drive up standards for all. Free schools and academies are welcomed as breaking the monopoly of local authority control and giving parents more power.

Alternative Provision: Home Schooling and De-schooling

Not all children are educated in formal school settings. Home schooling (also called home tuition) is legal in England and Wales. Parents who choose to home school must provide a suitable full-time education but are not required to follow the National Curriculum or sit public examinations.

The Austrian philosopher Ivan Illich went further, arguing in his 1971 work Deschooling Society that formal schooling is inherently oppressive and should be abolished altogether. De-schooling describes Illich’s vision of replacing compulsory institutions with “learning webs” — flexible networks where people learn what they want, when they want, from peers and community resources. Illich argued that schools impose a hidden curriculum of passivity and conformity, turning learners into consumers of packaged knowledge rather than independent thinkers.

Home schooling requires significant parental time, often a non-working parent, and resources for materials. Marxist sociologists would note that this makes it far more accessible to middle-class and wealthy families than working-class families, who may rely on both parents working full time. Home schooling is therefore not a neutral alternative — access to it is shaped by class position. Feminist sociologists would add that the expectation of home schooling often falls on mothers, reproducing the double shift and the gendered domestic division of labour.

Key Fact

Both academies and free schools are state-funded but operate outside local authority control. The key difference is their origin: academies are usually converted from existing state schools, while free schools are newly created by parents, charities or other groups. Both reflect the marketisation of education — the application of market principles to schooling.

lesson_title: Education and Capitalism: Bowles and Gintis
content_html:
Education and the Economy: A Marxist Analysis

Where functionalists see education as serving the whole of society, Marxist sociologists argue that it primarily serves the interests of the ruling class under capitalism. The most influential Marxist account of education is the correspondence principle, developed by Samuel Bowles and Herbert Gintis in their 1976 study Schooling in Capitalist America.

Key Fact

Bowles and Gintis argued that the social relationships in schools — between teachers and pupils, subjects and timetables — correspond closely to the social relationships workers experience in capitalist workplaces. Schools do not just teach academic skills; they socialise pupils into accepting hierarchy, obedience and routine.

The Correspondence Principle in Detail

In Schooling in Capitalist America (1976), Bowles and Gintis argued that schools mirror the workplace in several key ways. First, both schools and workplaces involve hierarchy and authority: pupils must obey teachers just as workers must obey managers. Second, in both settings, individuals receive external rewards for compliance — pupils receive grades; workers receive wages. Neither rewards are for genuine interest or intrinsic satisfaction, but for going through the motions.

Third, in both schools and workplaces, individuals have little meaningful control over the content of what they do: the curriculum is decided by others, just as workers do not decide what to produce. Fourth, school subjects are fragmented into separate lessons — mathematics, English, history — just as industrial production is divided into separate, specialised tasks. The overall effect, Bowles and Gintis argued, is that schools produce workers who are accustomed to taking orders, accepting hierarchy and suppressing their own creativity in the service of a system that benefits the bourgeoisie.

The Hidden Curriculum

Central to Bowles and Gintis’s argument is the concept of the hidden curriculum. The formal curriculum is the stated content of lessons — the subjects and skills explicitly taught. The hidden curriculum refers to the values, attitudes and behaviours that schools transmit implicitly: respect for authority, acceptance of hierarchy, punctuality, competition with peers, and the suppression of collective solidarity. Bowles and Gintis argued that these hidden lessons are more important than the formal content because they prepare workers to accept capitalist social relations without question.

The Myth of Meritocracy

A key element of the Bowles and Gintis argument is that the apparent meritocracy of education is, in practice, a myth. Because working-class pupils face material disadvantages at home — cramped housing, lack of educational resources, parents working long hours — they are less likely to achieve high grades even if they are equally talented. The education system then presents these unequal outcomes as the result of individual effort or ability, legitimising inequality. Those who “succeed” are seen as deserving their rewards; those who “fail” are told they simply did not try hard enough. The underlying class advantage is rendered invisible.

Functionalists do not deny that schools prepare young people for work — but they interpret this very differently. Parsons argued that schools transmit the values and skills society needs for its smooth functioning, and that the link between school and the economy is beneficial rather than exploitative. Where Bowles and Gintis see “obedience training”, functionalists see the teaching of necessary values like discipline, cooperation and punctuality that serve everyone, not just the ruling class. From a functionalist perspective, it is possible for meritocracy to be genuine: if schools truly operate on universalistic standards, talented pupils of any background can advance.

Feminist response: Feminists argue that Bowles and Gintis focus too narrowly on class and ignore gender. The hidden curriculum is also gendered: girls are socialised into compliance, modesty and caring roles; boys into competition and assertiveness. The correspondence principle reproduces not only class hierarchy but also patriarchy. The workplace that schools prepare pupils for is itself gendered — with women concentrated in lower-paid, caring and domestic roles.

Interactionist response: Interactionists argue that Bowles and Gintis present an overly deterministic account that treats pupils as passive recipients of socialisation. In practice, pupils do not simply absorb the hidden curriculum — they negotiate, resist and sometimes reject it. Paul Willis’s 1977 study Learning to Labour showed that working-class boys actively resisted the school’s authority rather than simply conforming. This active resistance is ignored in Bowles and Gintis’s model.

Key Fact

Bowles and Gintis published Schooling in Capitalist America in 1976. Their core claim was that the social relationships in schools (hierarchy, external rewards, fragmented tasks, lack of pupil autonomy) correspond to the social relationships of the capitalist workplace, producing compliant workers rather than free-thinking citizens.

Why Do Some Groups Achieve More Than Others?

Educational achievement in the UK is not evenly distributed. Statistical patterns consistently show that pupils from higher social classes outperform those from lower classes; girls have, since the 1990s, outperformed boys at GCSE and A level; and pupils from some ethnic minority backgrounds underperform relative to others. Sociologists disagree about the causes of these patterns — and offer competing explanations rooted in different perspectives.

Key Fact

The three main factors affecting educational achievement studied in GCSE Sociology are: social class, gender and ethnicity. For each factor, sociologists offer explanations at two levels: factors outside school (home background, material resources, cultural attitudes) and factors inside school (labelling, streaming, curriculum content).

Social Class and Achievement

Working-class pupils, on average, achieve lower grades at GCSE and are less likely to progress to university than middle-class pupils. Sociologists explain this gap in two main ways: material deprivation and cultural deprivation.

Material deprivation describes the economic disadvantages that working-class pupils face at home: overcrowded housing with no quiet space to study, inability to afford school uniforms or equipment, needing part-time jobs that reduce study time, and parents unable to pay for private tuition or educational visits. These material conditions make it harder to perform well regardless of ability or effort.

The concept of cultural capital was developed by the French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu. Bourdieu argued that middle-class families possess cultural capital — familiarity with the language, values and behaviours that schools reward. Middle-class children enter school already knowing how to speak to teachers, how to present work, and which cultural references to make. Working-class children often lack this cultural currency, which puts them at a systematic disadvantage even when they are equally able.

Halsey: Class Barriers and Origins and Destinations

A.H. Halsey’s study Origins and Destinations (conducted with Heath and Ridge, 1980) investigated the relationship between social class and educational achievement in Britain. Halsey found that despite the expansion of state education and the introduction of comprehensive schooling, class remained a powerful barrier to educational opportunity. Even when pupils of similar measured ability were compared, those from working-class backgrounds were significantly less likely to gain high-level qualifications or attend university. Halsey’s research challenged the optimistic functionalist claim that education had become genuinely meritocratic.

Ball: Parental Choice, Marketisation and Competition Between Schools

Stephen Ball’s research on marketisation and parental choice examined how the introduction of league tables, Ofsted inspections and open enrolment reshaped educational inequality. Ball argued that “parentocracy” — the rhetoric of parental choice — favours middle-class families who have the cultural capital and social networks to navigate the system: they know how to read league tables, visit multiple schools, write effective appeals and move house into desirable catchment areas. Working-class parents often make less “informed” choices — not because they care less, but because they lack access to the same information and resources. Ball’s research shows that market-based competition does not level the playing field; it gives already advantaged families further advantage.

Historically, boys outperformed girls in public examinations. Since the 1990s, this has reversed: girls now outperform boys at GCSE and A level on most measures. Feminist sociologists link girls’ improved performance to changes in female aspirations, the decline of traditionally male industries, and improvements in the curriculum that moved away from male-dominated content. Some sociologists argue that boys’ relative underachievement is linked to a “crisis of masculinity” — as traditional male manual jobs have declined, some working-class boys have come to see academic success as incompatible with masculine identity. Functionalists tend to see the gender gap as reflecting changing labour market needs; Marxist feminists argue it is complicated by both class and gender simultaneously.

Statistical data shows significant variation in achievement between different ethnic groups in the UK. Some groups — such as British Chinese and British Indian pupils — perform above the national average; others — such as Black Caribbean boys and White British working-class boys — perform below average. Sociologists offer competing explanations. The cultural deprivation thesis argues that some families transmit cultural values that are misaligned with school expectations. Critics argue this “blames the victim” and ignores structural explanations.

An alternative explanation focuses on the school itself. The ethnocentric curriculum — a curriculum that predominantly reflects White European culture and knowledge — may alienate minority ethnic pupils and undervalue their heritage. Institutional racism refers to discrimination that is embedded in the policies and practices of schools rather than in the attitudes of individual teachers. The Macpherson Report (1999), produced after the Stephen Lawrence Inquiry, introduced the concept of institutional racism into mainstream British public debate.

Key Fact

Material deprivation refers to a lack of financial resources (cramped housing, no study space, inability to pay for resources). Cultural deprivation refers to a lack of the attitudes, knowledge and behaviours schools reward. Both are associated with working-class underachievement, but they are distinct mechanisms — a pupil may face one without the other, and both can coexist.

What Happens Inside Schools?

Sociologists who focus on the macro level — class, capitalism, patriarchy — risk overlooking the daily processes within schools that shape individual outcomes. Interactionist sociologists argue that what happens in classrooms and corridors — how teachers perceive and label pupils, how pupils are grouped, how peer cultures develop — has a profound effect on achievement that cannot be explained solely by external factors such as class or home background.

Key Fact

Processes within schools that affect educational achievement include: streaming, setting, mixed ability teaching, labelling and the self-fulfilling prophecy.

Streaming and Setting

Many secondary schools in England allocate pupils to different ability groups. Streaming places pupils in a fixed group for all subjects, based on an overall assessment of ability. Setting places pupils in different groups for individual subjects, allowing for movement between groups as performance changes. Some schools use mixed ability teaching, keeping pupils of all abilities together in the same class.

From a functionalist perspective, streaming and setting allow teachers to pitch lessons at the appropriate level for each group, potentially improving efficiency. From an interactionist perspective, the process is more problematic. Once pupils are placed in a low stream or set, teachers may have lower expectations of them, offer them less challenging work, and interact with them differently. The pupils themselves may internalise the label “low ability” and adjust their own aspirations accordingly.

Ball on Banding and Teacher Expectations

Stephen Ball’s study Beachside Comprehensive (1981) investigated the introduction and effects of banding in a fictional comprehensive school (referred to as “Beachside”). Ball found that the band a pupil was placed in at the start of secondary school significantly shaped their educational trajectory, regardless of their actual ability. Pupils in the lower bands received a less academic curriculum, had lower teacher expectations placed on them, and developed more negative attitudes towards school. Ball’s research showed that the act of grouping pupils by ability was not a neutral administrative decision but a process laden with social consequences, particularly for working-class pupils who were disproportionately placed in lower bands.

Labelling Theory and the Self-Fulfilling Prophecy

Labelling theory, associated with interactionist sociologists, argues that the definitions and categories that teachers attach to pupils have real consequences for those pupils’ futures. When a teacher identifies a pupil as “bright”, “disruptive”, “lazy” or “hard-working”, this label shapes subsequent interactions: the pupil receives more (or less) encouragement, is called on more (or less) frequently in class, and is treated differently in disciplinary situations.

This process can produce a self-fulfilling prophecy: a pupil labelled as “high ability” begins to internalise that identity and works hard to fulfil expectations; a pupil labelled as “low ability” or “a troublemaker” may disengage from school, accept the label and behave accordingly. The original label — which may have been based on class, ethnicity or gender prejudice rather than genuine ability — becomes self-confirming. Howard Becker’s broader interactionist work on master status is relevant here: once a pupil is labelled as “a problem”, that label can become their master status, colouring every interaction they have with teachers and other pupils.

Paul Willis’s 1977 ethnographic study Learning to Labour followed twelve working-class boys (whom Willis called “the lads”) in a West Midlands comprehensive school in the mid-1970s. Willis found that “the lads” developed a counter-school culture: a system of values that actively opposed the school’s emphasis on academic work, obedience and qualifications. The lads saw conformist “ear’oles” (pupils who accepted the school’s rules) as passive and weak. The lads valued masculine physical toughness, resistance to authority and the anticipation of manual labour — the very traits that would lead them into working-class factory jobs.

Willis’s study is significant for several reasons. First, it challenged Bowles and Gintis by showing that working-class pupils are not passive: they actively resist the school’s authority rather than being socialised into compliance. Second, it showed that this very resistance — which the lads experienced as freedom and rebellion — ultimately prepared them for working-class jobs just as effectively as conformity did. Third, Willis drew on interactionist ideas about peer culture while framing his analysis within a Marxist concern with class reproduction.

Functionalist: Streaming and setting are rational, efficient responses to differences in pupil ability. They allow teachers to target teaching appropriately and ensure that the most able pupils are stretched. The process is seen as broadly meritocratic, matching pupils to future roles based on demonstrated ability.

Interactionist: Labels attached by teachers shape pupils’ identities and trajectories through the self-fulfilling prophecy. Banding and streaming are not neutral — they reflect and reinforce teacher judgements that are often shaped by class, gender and ethnicity (Ball’s Beachside research). The focus is on micro-level classroom interactions.

Marxist: Processes within schools are mechanisms of class reproduction. Counter-school cultures (Willis) arise because working-class pupils recognise — at some level — that the meritocracy claim is hollow. Streaming channels working-class pupils towards lower expectations and lesser credentials, reproducing the class structure.

Feminist: Labels and expectations are also gendered. Teachers may expect girls to be quieter, more compliant and less mathematically able, and boys to be noisier, more disruptive and more suited to sciences. These gendered expectations shape behaviour and subject choice, reproducing occupational gender segregation.

Key Fact

Labelling comes first: a teacher (or peer) attaches a label to a pupil (“trouble-maker”, “high achiever”). The self-fulfilling prophecy describes what happens next: the pupil internalises the label and begins to act in ways that confirm it, so the original prediction comes true regardless of whether it was accurate initially.

Why Does Research Method Matter in Education?

All the sociological knowledge discussed in this unit — from Bowles and Gintis on the correspondence principle to Willis on counter-school cultures — rests on research conducted in and about schools. The choice of research method shapes what a sociologist can find out. Different methods provide different types of data, carry different practical difficulties, and raise different ethical issues — particularly when the research subjects are children.

Key Fact

Sociologists researching education use a range of methods: observation (participant or non-participant), interviews (structured, unstructured or focus group), questionnaires and secondary data such as official statistics and league tables.

Observation in Schools

Participant observation involves the researcher joining the group being studied — in the school context, sitting in classrooms, spending time in corridors and the playground, and building relationships with pupils and teachers over time. Willis’s Learning to Labour (1977) is the most celebrated example: Willis spent an extended period observing twelve working-class boys at a West Midlands comprehensive, attending lessons, factory visits and informal gatherings. The strength of this approach is validity: by immersing himself in the lads’ world, Willis gained rich, in-depth data about their attitudes, values and daily lives that a questionnaire could not have produced.

Non-participant observation involves watching what happens in classrooms or school settings without joining the group. This is less likely to change participants’ behaviour than participant observation, but it generates less detailed insight into participants’ meanings and motivations. Ball’s Beachside Comprehensive research used observation alongside interviews to investigate how banding shaped teachers’ expectations and pupils’ trajectories.

A key weakness of participant observation in schools is the risk of researcher influence: the presence of an adult observer in a classroom changes the dynamic between teachers and pupils. Teachers may behave more professionally; pupils may perform or act up for the observer. This undermines validity. There is also a significant practical issue: gaining sustained access to classrooms and pupils requires agreement from headteachers, class teachers and — for minors — parents.

Interviews in Education Research

Interviews allow sociologists to explore participants’ perspectives in depth. Unstructured interviews — open-ended conversations guided by a broad topic rather than fixed questions — are particularly effective for exploring sensitive topics like the experience of being labelled by a teacher, or attitudes to school among disengaged pupils. They produce rich qualitative data.

Halsey’s Origins and Destinations research combined survey data with follow-up interviews to investigate the relationship between class background and educational achievement. This mixed-methods approach used triangulation — checking findings from one method against another — to increase confidence in the conclusions.

Interviewing pupils presents specific practical and ethical challenges. Young people may give socially desirable answers — saying what they think the interviewer wants to hear rather than what they genuinely think. Interviewing pupils about sensitive topics (experience of racism, bullying, family poverty) requires careful attention to confidentiality and potential harm.

Official Statistics and League Tables

Sociologists researching educational achievement frequently use official statistics: GCSE and A-level results data published by the Department for Education, Ofsted inspection reports, and national league tables. These sources are large-scale, longitudinal and freely available, allowing researchers to identify trends in achievement across social class, gender and ethnicity over time — as Halsey’s research did.

However, official statistics must be treated with caution. League tables measure exam results but not the value a school adds to pupils’ progress. A school serving a predominantly disadvantaged intake may achieve lower grades than one serving a middle-class catchment, but may in fact be more effective. Ofsted inspection judgements are shaped by the criteria inspectors apply, which can change over time, and by who is doing the inspecting. Sociologists note that these statistics are socially constructed — they reflect decisions about what to measure and how, and should not be treated as objective truths about school quality.

Gaining access to schools is a major practical challenge for educational researchers. Schools are hierarchical institutions with formal gatekeepers: the headteacher must agree to the research, then individual class teachers must agree to open their classrooms, and parents must give consent for their children to participate. Each level of gatekeeping can limit or shape what the researcher can observe or ask about. Headteachers may refuse access to classrooms where teaching is poor; they may only allow researchers to observe “good” lessons, distorting the data.

Ofsted inspections also shape school behaviour: schools may change their routines and display pupils’ best work in the run-up to an inspection, meaning that data collected immediately before or after an inspection may not be representative of everyday school life. Time and cost are further practical issues: qualitative studies like Willis’s require months of fieldwork and close personal involvement, making them expensive and difficult to replicate.

Informed consent is particularly complex when research subjects are children. Because children are minors, sociologists must usually obtain consent from both the child and their parent or guardian. However, requiring parental consent can reduce the sample to pupils whose parents are engaged and willing to respond, which may introduce class bias. Children should also be told clearly what the research involves and that they can withdraw at any time.

Confidentiality means that the researcher must protect participants’ identities. Willis called his school “Hammertown”; Ball used the pseudonym “Beachside”. Pupils who confide in a researcher about negative experiences — bullying, poverty, difficult family situations — must be assured that their names will not be identifiable in any publication. However, confidentiality must be balanced against the duty to report serious safeguarding concerns.

Harm to participants includes psychological harm: asking pupils to discuss experiences of labelling, exclusion or racism may cause distress. Researchers should use sensitive interview techniques, provide the opportunity for debriefing, and ensure that pupils know they can stop at any time. Covert observation raises additional ethical concerns: participants do not know they are being studied and cannot give informed consent.

Key Fact

The three key ethical issues in sociological research are informed consent (especially complex with child participants — parental consent also required), confidentiality (protecting participants’ identities — Willis and Ball both used pseudonyms for their schools) and harm to participants (psychological distress from sensitive questions; balanced against the duty to report safeguarding concerns).

lesson_title: The Social Construction of Crime and Deviance
content_html:
Crime and Deviance: Two Distinct Concepts

One of the first distinctions sociology asks you to make is between crime and deviance. These concepts overlap but are not the same thing. A crime is an act that breaks the formal law; deviance is any behaviour that violates the unwritten social norms of a group or society. Many deviant acts are not criminal — queue-jumping, belching loudly in a restaurant or wearing a swimsuit to a funeral all break social expectations but carry no legal penalty. Equally, some criminal acts are not widely regarded as deviant — many motorists who exceed the speed limit by a small amount do not consider themselves “criminals” in any meaningful social sense.

This distinction matters because sociology treats both crime and deviance as social constructs — they are not fixed, objective categories but are defined and redefined by societies, institutions and individuals over time.

Key Fact

Crime and deviance are related but distinct: crime breaks the formal law; deviance violates social norms. Some acts are only one of these; only some are both. Sociology studies both as social constructs that change across time, place and situation.

Formal and Informal Rules

Societies regulate behaviour through two types of rules. Formal rules are codified in law and backed by state sanctions: fines, imprisonment or community service. Informal rules — sometimes called social norms — govern everyday behaviour through informal pressure: social disapproval, ridicule or exclusion from the group. A student who arrives late to every lesson is breaking an informal norm; a student who commits fraud is breaking a formal rule. Both are forms of deviance in the sociological sense, but only the second is a crime.

Societies use sanctions to enforce both types of rules. Positive sanctions reward conformity (a round of applause, a pay rise, social praise); negative sanctions punish deviation (a fine, a prison sentence, social exclusion). The relationship between formal law and informal norms is itself a sociological question: laws tend to reflect the norms of the dominant groups in society, a point Marxist and feminist perspectives challenge.

The Relativity of Deviance

A key insight of sociology is that deviance is relative: what counts as deviant varies across time, place and social situation. Three dimensions of relativity are particularly important.

Across time: Acts that were once legal can become criminal — fox hunting with dogs was a lawful rural tradition in England and Wales until the Hunting Act 2004 made it a criminal offence. Conversely, acts once treated as crimes can be decriminalised or legalised — homosexual acts between consenting adult men were criminal offences in England and Wales until the Sexual Offences Act 1967 partially decriminalised them. The law changes as the values and power structures of society change.

Across place: The same act may be legal in one country but criminal in another. Cannabis possession is legal for recreational use in the Netherlands under certain conditions but remains a criminal offence in England and Wales. Drinking alcohol in a public place is unremarkable in most of the United Kingdom but constitutes a serious offence in countries that enforce strict religious law. These cross-cultural variations demonstrate that crime is not an inherent property of an act but a label applied by a society.

Across situation: Context shapes whether an act is considered deviant. Killing another person is treated as murder in most contexts but may be regarded as heroic in warfare, or legally permitted as self-defence. A surgeon cutting open a patient's body with a scalpel is performing a legitimate medical procedure; the same action outside that context would be an assault. Interactionist sociologists like Becker emphasised that deviance is not a quality of the act itself but is created by the reactions of audiences to the act.

Sociological Perspectives on the Social Construction of Crime

Different sociological perspectives explain the social construction of crime in contrasting ways, reflecting deeper disagreements about the nature of society.

A very common examination error is to treat crime and deviance as synonyms. They are overlapping but distinct categories. The simplest way to keep them separate is to think of two overlapping circles: the left circle is all criminal acts, the right circle is all deviant acts. The overlap in the middle is acts that are both criminal and widely seen as deviant (such as violent assault). The left-only region is acts that are criminal but not seen as deviant by most people (minor speeding). The right-only region is acts that are deviant but not criminal (being rude to a stranger). On an exam question asking you to “define deviance”, giving a legal definition will lose marks.

Functionalist perspective: From a functionalist viewpoint, crime and deviance are defined relative to the value consensus of society. Durkheim argued that some level of crime is normal and even functional in any society — it helps clarify the boundaries of acceptable behaviour and, when punished, reaffirms shared values. On this view, defining something as “criminal” is the community expressing its moral boundaries.

Marxist perspective: Marxist sociologists argue that criminal law is not a neutral reflection of shared values but an instrument of class power. The bourgeoisie shape the law to protect their property and interests, criminalising acts common among the working class (street theft) while failing to criminalise or leniently treating harmful acts by the powerful (corporate fraud, tax evasion). The social construction of “crime” therefore reflects and reinforces class inequality.

Feminist perspective: Feminist sociologists point out that laws have historically been made predominantly by men and have often reflected patriarchal interests. Many acts of violence against women — marital rape, for instance — were not defined as criminal in England and Wales until relatively recently (rape within marriage was only conclusively criminalised in R v R, 1991). Definitions of crime and deviance therefore embed gender power relations, and feminist research examines how the social construction of crime affects women both as victims and as offenders.

Interactionist perspective: Interactionists such as Becker argue that no act is inherently criminal or deviant; it becomes so only when a label is successfully applied to it by someone with the power to make the label stick. The social construction of crime is an ongoing process of labelling, negotiation and reaction. Becker used the term moral entrepreneurs to describe individuals and groups who actively campaign for certain behaviours to be defined as deviant or criminal — pressure groups lobbying for new legislation are a contemporary example.

Key Fact

Four perspectives explain social construction differently: functionalists see crime as defined by shared values; Marxists see law as serving the ruling class; feminists see law as historically shaped by patriarchal power; interactionists focus on labelling as the mechanism by which acts become “criminal” or “deviant”.

Law and Morality: Are They the Same?

A final dimension of the social construction of crime is the relationship between law and morality. Not everything that is morally condemned is illegal, and not everything that is illegal is morally condemned by all members of society. Lying to a friend is widely regarded as morally wrong but carries no legal penalty. Some individuals regard civil disobedience — breaking an unjust law — as a moral act. The gap between law and morality varies across time and culture and is itself a product of social processes. Sociologists are interested in who gets to define the law, whose morality it encodes, and whose behaviour it criminalises — questions that run through the entire sociology of crime and deviance.

content_html:
Durkheim: Crime Is Normal and Functional

Functionalist sociology begins from the premise that society works like a living organism: its institutions perform necessary functions and, when working well, produce social order and value consensus. Emile Durkheim argued that crime is not simply a social problem to be eliminated — it is a normal feature of every known society. If crime were to disappear entirely, Durkheim reasoned, society would have become so rigid and repressive that even the most minor non-conformity would be treated as a serious offence. A healthy society requires a certain level of deviance to function.

Durkheim identified two functions of crime. First, crime performs a boundary maintenance function: when an offender is publicly punished, the community gathers around the shared moral boundary that has been violated, reaffirming collective values. Court proceedings, media coverage of verdicts and public discussion of serious crimes all serve this ritual function. Second, crime can act as a driver of social change: acts that are initially labelled criminal — civil rights protests, for example — may eventually prompt a rethinking of the law. Yesterday’s criminal can become tomorrow’s reformer.

Durkheim also introduced the concept of anomie — a state of normlessness that arises when the rules holding society together break down. For Durkheim, periods of rapid social change (economic booms or slumps) could weaken the norms that regulate individual desires, leading to an increase in deviant behaviour. Robert Merton later developed this concept into a full theory of crime.

Key Fact

Durkheim argued crime performs two functions for society: boundary maintenance (reaffirming shared values through punishment) and enabling social change (challenging unjust laws). He also introduced anomie — normlessness resulting from the breakdown of social rules.

Merton: Strain Theory and the Goals–Means Gap

Robert Merton, writing in Social Theory and Social Structure (1938, enlarged 1968), developed Durkheim’s concept of anomie into a systematic theory of crime. Merton argued that deviance results from the culture and structure of society — not from individual pathology or moral failure.

Merton started from the functionalist premise of value consensus: all members of society are socialised into the same cultural goals, particularly the goal of material success. However, because members of society have different positions in the social structure, they do not have equal access to the institutionalised means — the legitimate routes (education, employment, talent) through which success is achieved. Members of the working class and poor communities are socialised into the same aspirations as everyone else but face far greater structural barriers to achieving them.

This gap between cultural goals and institutionalised means creates a strain that puts pressure on individuals to deviate. Crucially, Merton believed that in American society (the context of his original research, though his ideas have wide application) the emphasis on success far outweighed the emphasis on achieving it legitimately — “winning at all costs” encouraged a state of anomie in which the usual rules governing behaviour were abandoned. The concept can be applied in a UK context: the expectation of consumer lifestyle success is widely promoted through media and advertising, yet structural barriers (class inequality, educational inequalities) mean that not all routes to that success are equally available.

Merton’s Five Responses to Strain

Merton identified five ways in which individuals can respond to the tension between cultural goals and the available means to achieve them. These are not personality types but modes of adaptation to social structure.

1. Conformity: Accepts both the cultural goals (material success) and the institutionalised means (education, employment). This is the most common adaptation and produces social stability. The conformist works hard, gains qualifications and pursues a career within the rules of the system.

2. Innovation: Accepts the cultural goals but rejects or lacks access to the legitimate means. The individual turns instead to deviant or criminal methods — theft, fraud, drug dealing. Merton argued that innovation was most common among those lower in the class structure who faced the greatest gap between aspirations and opportunities. This is the response most directly linked to crime.

3. Ritualism: Rejects or abandons the cultural goals (no longer striving for wealth and success) but continues to follow the institutionalised means rigidly. The ritualist remains in a low-paid, low-status job and follows the rules to the letter — perhaps through an enthusiasm for petty bureaucracy — without expecting advancement. Merton associated this with some middle-class individuals who have been strongly socialised to conform but have little prospect of upward mobility.

4. Retreatism: Rejects both the cultural goals and the means of achieving them. The retreatist “drops out” of society altogether, withdrawing from mainstream life. Merton applied this concept to explain the behaviour of people experiencing chronic poverty, homelessness or long-term addiction. This adaptation involves neither conventional success nor criminal gain — simply withdrawal.

5. Rebellion: Rejects both existing cultural goals and means but replaces them with alternative goals and means. Unlike the retreatist, the rebel acts to create a new social order. Merton saw this as typical of members of a “rising class” who may attempt organised political revolt or social revolution.

Key Fact

Merton’s five responses: Conformity (accepts goals + means), Innovation (accepts goals, rejects means — most linked to crime), Ritualism (rejects goals, accepts means), Retreatism (rejects both), Rebellion (rejects both, substitutes new goals and means).

Subcultural Theories: Albert Cohen

Albert Cohen, in Delinquent Boys (1955), extended the strain tradition but shifted focus from individual adaptation to collective, subcultural responses. Cohen argued that working-class boys hold the same success goals as the wider society but, because of cultural deprivation and poor educational prospects, they consistently fail to achieve by mainstream standards.

This failure produces what Cohen called status frustration. Rather than innovating individually (Merton’s route), working-class boys respond collectively by forming delinquent subcultures that invert the mainstream values they have been denied: they celebrate vandalism, truancy and theft not because these acts gain material wealth but because they gain status and prestige within the subculture. Success at what the mainstream condemns becomes a source of peer recognition.

Cohen’s approach adds an important dimension missing from Merton’s theory: it explains non-instrumental crime — acts committed not for economic gain but for status, thrill or group belonging. Critics of Cohen argue that not all working-class boys experience school failure in the same way, and that his account overlooks girls and young women entirely. Feminist and interactionist perspectives offer different explanations for why subcultures form along gendered lines.

Evaluating Functionalist and Subcultural Theories

Merton’s strain theory has been influential because it shifts blame for crime from individuals to the social structure. However, critics point out several limitations. Marxist sociologists argue that Merton fails to ask who makes the laws and who benefits from them: focusing on working-class innovation ignores corporate crime, tax evasion and white-collar offending. Interactionist critics argue that Merton assumes a single value system (success goals) shared by all, when in practice values vary across class, gender and ethnicity. Feminist critics note that Merton’s theory is largely silent on women and crime. Cohen has been criticised for overstating cultural deprivation as the cause of working-class failure and for producing an account that applies only to young males in urban settings.

Students sometimes write “anomie means crime.” Anomie is the condition — a state of normlessness or the breakdown of social rules — not the criminal behaviour itself. Crime (specifically innovation in Merton’s framework) is one possible response to anomie, but conformity, retreatism and other adaptations are also responses to the same condition. Always define anomie as normlessness or the breakdown of rules, then explain how it can lead to deviance.

lesson_title: Interactionist Theory of Crime: Becker and Labelling
content_html:
The Interactionist Challenge

Functionalist and structural theories ask why certain social conditions (strain, status frustration, class inequality) lead to crime. Interactionist sociology asks a different question: who decides what counts as criminal or deviant in the first place, and what happens to individuals once they are labelled? This shift of focus — from the causes of rule-breaking to the social processes of labelling — produced one of the most influential perspectives in the sociology of crime.

Interactionism argues that social reality is constructed through interaction and the meanings people assign to actions. Applied to crime and deviance, this means that an act has no inherent criminal quality — it becomes deviant only when someone with the power to make the label stick successfully defines it as such.

Becker: Labelling Theory

Howard Becker, in Outsiders (1963), set out the foundational argument of labelling theory. Becker argued that deviance is not a property of the act itself but of the interaction between the person who acts and those who observe and respond to the act. Whether a label of “deviant” or “criminal” is applied depends on who commits the act, when and where it is committed, who observes it, and the negotiations between the various parties involved.

Becker observed that not all rule-breakers are caught, and not all who are caught are labelled. Whether a label sticks depends on factors beyond the act itself: the social characteristics of the actor (class, ethnicity, age, gender), the discretion of those with formal power (police, teachers, courts), and the social context. Two young people committing the same act may receive very different responses depending on where they are and who they are. Becker’s insight was that the criminal justice system is not a neutral machine but a social process shaped by power.

Key Fact

Becker (Outsiders, 1963) argued that deviance is not a property of the act but is created by the reactions of others. An act only becomes deviant when a label is successfully applied by someone with the power to make it stick.

Master Status and the Deviant Career

Once a label has been publicly and officially applied, Becker argued, it tends to become the person’s master status. Before the label, a young person might be seen as a student, a friend, a neighbour. After being officially convicted and labelled a “criminal”, this identity overshadows all others. Assumptions are made about the person’s character, reliability and likely future behaviour — assumptions that can follow them into every interaction: with employers, with landlords, with teachers, with family members.

The consequences of master status may trigger what Becker described as a deviant career. As the labelled individual is rejected from legitimate social roles — turned down by employers, excluded from educational opportunities, cut off from conventional social networks — the label itself makes conventional life harder to sustain. This rejection can produce a self-fulfilling prophecy: the individual increasingly identifies with the label and seeks out others who share it, joining organised deviant groups with their own norms, values and identity. In this way, the labelling process can transform an isolated act of rule-breaking into an ongoing criminal lifestyle — not because the individual was inevitably going to become a criminal, but because the social reaction created the conditions for it.

Primary and Secondary Deviance

Primary deviance refers to the original act of rule-breaking, before any label has been applied. Most people commit acts of primary deviance at some point (minor theft, underage drinking, breaking traffic rules) without it becoming part of their identity. Secondary deviance occurs when an individual internalises the deviant label and begins to act in accordance with it. The distinction is important: the theory argues that secondary deviance is produced not by the original act but by the social reaction to it.

Moral Entrepreneurs and Moral Panics

Becker also introduced the concept of moral entrepreneurs — individuals and groups who use their social influence to get particular behaviours defined as deviant. They may lobby parliament for new legislation, campaign in the media, or pressure institutions to act. Their success depends on their social power and their ability to frame the issue in ways that resonate with public anxieties.

Related to this is the concept of a moral panic. When the media, police and public respond to a perceived threat in a disproportionate and amplified way, the resulting attention can itself increase the visible scale of the problem through a process of deviancy amplification: increased police attention leads to more arrests, which generates more media coverage, which fuels further anxiety and policing. The labelling process escalates. Critics argue that moral panics have historically targeted specific groups (young working-class men, ethnic minority communities) who are portrayed as “folk devils” — symbols of social threat.

Feminist perspective: Feminist sociologists broadly welcome the insight that labelling is not neutral. Heidensohn noted that the criminal justice system has historically applied labels differently to men and women: women offenders are sometimes treated more leniently (the “chivalry thesis”) when they conform to feminine stereotypes, but women who deviate from expected gender roles may be judged more harshly. Feminist criminologists argue that the identity of the label-appliers — predominantly male judges, police and juries — shapes who is targeted and how they are treated.

Marxist perspective: Marxist sociologists argue that labelling theory does not go far enough because it focuses on individual interactions without asking why the police and courts are more likely to label working-class people as criminal. The answer, for Marxists, lies in the class structure: the bourgeoisie controls the legal system and ensures that the label “criminal” is attached primarily to acts associated with the proletariat (street crime, theft, benefit fraud) rather than to the far more costly but largely tolerated crimes of the powerful (corporate fraud, tax avoidance, environmental damage). Selective law enforcement reflects and reinforces class inequality.

Key Fact

Labelling theory has been criticised from multiple directions: Marxists argue it doesn’t explain why labels fall on the working class (class power); feminists argue gender shapes both labelling and its consequences; critics also note that not everyone who is labelled accepts or acts on the label (determinism).

Strengths: Labelling theory challenges the view that crime statistics are an objective reflection of criminal behaviour, showing instead that they reflect the activities of the police and courts. It draws attention to the unequal application of labels across social groups. It helps explain patterns such as recidivism (re-offending after conviction), which purely structural theories struggle to account for.

Weaknesses: Labelling theory has been criticised for being too deterministic — not everyone who is labelled becomes a career criminal; many labelled individuals resist and reject the identity. It focuses on the label-givers (police, courts) but underplays the role of the actor’s own choices and motivations. Functionalists argue that labelling theory cannot explain why some acts (serious violence) are universally condemned regardless of the social identity of the actor.
